title: Tissue-wide single-cell CRISPR screening for microproteins unveils hidden layers of ribosomal complexity - Nature Cell Biology
byline: Valdivia-Francia; Fabiola; Rabl; Julius; Muzumdar; Sukalp; Khandekar; Ameya; Pfammatter; Sibylle; Renz; Peter F; Spies; Daniel; Ormiston; Mark; Hyams; Katie; We
html:
Abstract

The dark proteome comprises a rapidly expanding catalogue of microproteins with largely unknown functions. Here we exploit an in vivo single-cell CRISPR screening strategy in the mouse epidermis to systematically investigate their tissue-wide function. We document the global and cell-type-specific roles of microproteins at single-cell transcriptomic resolution and identify a cohort of functional ribosomal protein-like microproteins. We characterize a microprotein on Gm10076, identical to the ribosomal intersubunit bridge protein RPL41, whose perturbation strongly impairs protein synthesis. Cryo-electron microscopy reveals that, unlike canonical RPL41, Gm10076-encoded RPL41 is not incorporated into the intersubunit bridge but localizes to the nucleolus. Comparative translational profiling of Gm10076 and Rpl41 knockouts indicates that Gm10076 loss alters the translational efficiency of ribosome biogenesis factors and disrupts coordination of 40S and 60S maturation programs. Together, our study charts the tissue-wide functional landscape of the dark proteome and implicates transcript context-dependent diversification of identical microproteins in shaping translational landscapes.

Main

The mammalian genome encompasses numerous non-canonical microprotein-encoding open reading frames (ORFs), which have been historically overlooked in genome annotations. Traditional annotation methods for protein-coding ORFs in genomes focused on specific criteria, such as minimum length standards or amino acid conservation. This led to the exclusion of proteins shorter than 100 amino acids, which were dismissed as non-functional. However, recent genome-wide ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry (MS) studies have challenged the traditional annotation of ORFs, resulting in the identification of more than 7,200 human non-canonical ORFs that encode microproteins, thereby substantially expanding the protein-coding capacity of a cell1,2.

Although the number of annotated microproteins is rapidly increasing, only a small fraction have been functionally characterized2,3. Microprotein function has been reported in diverse cellular processes, highlighting their biological activity in cellular signalling, gene regulation and metabolism4,5,6,7,8. In addition, microproteins may play widespread roles in driving the pathogenesis of diseases such as cancer, highlighted by pan-cancer analyses with thousands of microprotein transcripts deregulated in cancer4,9. However, the extent to which microproteins impact cellular function and how these roles vary in a cell-type-specific manner remains largely unknown. Understanding the contributions of microproteins to tissue function necessitates robust in vivo platforms that can systematically map microprotein functions in specific cell types.

Pooled CRISPR screens represent a powerful strategy to investigate the function of microproteins and have spurred the identification of functionally relevant microproteins10,11,12,13,14. Although highly effective, pooled CRISPR screens have two major limitations. First, they are restricted to simple cellular readouts such as proliferation and cannot capture more complex cellular traits such as transcriptomics, which are among the most comprehensive characterizations of cellular function. Second, pooled CRISPR screens are unable to assess cell-type-specific roles of microproteins. Uncovering cell-type-specific microprotein functions could enhance our understanding of how microproteins contribute to the complexity of mammalian proteomes.

Here, we exploit the mouse epidermis as a model to systematically dissect the tissue-wide function of microproteins at single-cell transcriptomic resolution. We employ ultrasound-guided in utero microinjections of lentiviral libraries into embryonic stage (E) 9.5 embryos and combine it with an adjusted CRISPR droplet sequencing (CROP-seq) strategy to document the cell-type-specific function of microproteins15,16. We unveil a long noncoding RNA (lncRNA)-derived RPL41 microprotein that is identical to canonical RPL41, yet differs in function and is essential for cellular translation and proliferation.

Results

Annotation of non-canonical ORFs from ribosome profiling data

To annotate translated non-canonical ORFs in healthy tissues and cancer, we first set out to analyse our own and published sets of ribosome profiling data of the mouse skin17. We exploited the ORF regression algorithm for translational evaluation of ribosome-protected footprints (ORF-RATER)18, thereby determining all possible ORFs with canonical and near-cognate start codons regardless of minimum length. Using ORF-RATER, we annotated ORFs in both wild-type and pre-oncogenic SOX2-expressing mouse epidermis in vivo, as well as in wild-type keratinocytes and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) cells in vitro (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). Furthermore, we included translation initiation sites from harringtonine-treated samples, which blocks initiating but not elongating ribosomes19 (Fig. 1a).

a, The workflow for annotating non-canonical ORFs from mouse ribosome profiling datasets. ORFs were classified using the ORF-RATER pipeline into three main categories: annotated ORFs, variant ORFs and novel ORFs. b, Pie charts showing the percentage of ORFs with ATG, CTG, GTG or TTG start codons across different ORF categories. Although other start sites have been reported, we only included these start codons. c, A cumulative fraction plot showing the length distribution of ORFs. Overall, 76% of novel ORFs are shorter than 100 amino acids. d, A schematic of the single-cell CRISPR screen to identify functional microproteins. A pooled library containing 720 sgRNAs was injected in utero into the amniotic cavity of E9.5 Pik3caH1047R+/− Cas9+/− embryos. Skin was collected at postnatal day 4 (P4) and day 60 (P60), and GFP-positive cells were sorted for scRNA-seq and sgRNA capture. e, The distribution of GFP-positive clones in sections of the P60 epidermis. E-cadherin staining marks epithelial cell junctions. Dashed lines mark GFP-positive clones. Images are representative of n = 4 sections from 3 mice. f, Wholemount immunofluorescence of GFP-positive clones in the P60 mouse epidermis. E-cadherin staining marks epithelial cell junctions. Images are representative of n = 3 biological replicates. SCC, squamous cell carcinoma; uORFs, upstream ORFs.

We identified a total of 22,404 ORFs, among which 12,011 (54%) were recognized as annotated canonical ORFs. Overall, 7,378 (33%) of the identified ORFs were variants of annotated ORFs. Finally, we identified 3,015 (13%) novel ORFs, including 1,269 upstream ORFs (uORF), 851 new ORFs, 99 novel ORFs on alternative isoforms (new_iso), 779 internal ORFs and 17 downstream ORFs (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). The representative ribosome profiling traces from newly identified microproteins showed similar footprint patterns as those from annotated coding sequences (CDSs), including the presence of triplet-nucleotide periodicity, which is a hallmark feature of translation (Extended Data Fig. 1d–g and Supplementary Fig. 1).

Overall, 99.8% of canonical CDSs initiated with an AUG codon, while 49% of the novel ORFs utilized near-cognate start sites (NUG, where N represents C, G or U), with CUG being the most prevalent start codon (Fig. 1b). For uORFs, 29% start with a near-cognate start codon, while 66% of the new ORFs initiate with non-AUG codons. Canonical ORFs had the longest median length at 338 codons, followed by variant ORFs with a median length of 240 codons and novel ORFs, which had a median length of 26 codons. Within novel ORFs, median lengths ranged from 15 codons for uORFs, 21 codons for internal ORFs, 43 codons for newly identified ORFs and up to 59 codons for downstream ORFs (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1h).

Prompted by the predicted translation of 3,015 novel ORFs, we set out to investigate the function of the identified uORFs and new ORFs (herein, both referred to as microproteins). We curated a high-confidence subset of predicted microproteins using the ORF-RATER rank-sum approach, which ranks ORFs on the basis of translation features (Supplementary Table 1). Given their potential relevance to cancer, we prioritized microproteins highly translated in pre-oncogenic and oncogenic genetic backgrounds. This selection included a total of 156 uORFs and 65 new ORFs. In addition, we included eight known uORFs within Atf4 (two uORFs), Mief1, Mdm2, Ctnnb1, Hras and Pten (two uORFs) transcripts. Finally, 50 non-targeting single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) were included as controls.

In vivo single-cell CRISPR to target microproteins

To test the function of microproteins, we exploited our recently established in vivo single-cell CRISPR screening strategy to infer tissue-wide gene function in the mouse epidermis15. This technique leverages ultrasound-guided microinjections of lentiviral libraries into E9.5 embryos and enables us to link the perturbation of microproteins to its single-cell transcriptomic response15,20,21 (Fig. 1d). The system integrates the sgRNA into a polymerase II-driven transcript for direct capture by single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq)16. To explore the roles of microproteins within a cancer-relevant genetic context, we used an inducible Pik3ca mouse model carrying the H1047R hotspot mutation, a recurrent alteration in human cancers22,23 (Fig. 1d) that has been previously exploited as a sensitized oncogenic background for screens24,25. We then crossed this cancer model with the inducible Cas9-EGFP mouse to allow gene editing of microproteins. For recombination, we substituted the puromycin cassette in the original CROP-seq vector with a Cre recombinase, thereby enabling simultaneous Cre-dependent expression of oncogenic PIK3CA and CAS9 in infected cells (Fig. 1d), while infected cells can be tracked via green fluorescent protein (EGFP) expression (Fig. 1d–f and Extended Data Fig. 1i).

To determine the function of microproteins, we subcloned the library of 720 sgRNAs targeting 229 microproteins into our adjusted CROP-seq Cre vector, with three sgRNAs per microprotein (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 2). However, owing to the scarcity of NGG motifs required for the CRISPR system, some microproteins shorter than 45 nucleotides were targeted with only two sgRNAs (Supplementary Table 2). Given the limited design options for selecting high-efficiency sgRNAs, we tested the editing efficiency of 45 sgRNAs. While 21 out of 45 demonstrated robust editing (>25% editing efficiency), their overall efficiency was, as expected, lower than that typically observed for sgRNAs targeting conventional genes15 (Extended Data Fig. 2). We then produced high-titre lentivirus and used the in utero ultrasound-guided microinjection system to deliver the library into the amniotic cavity of E9.5 mouse embryos. At this stage, the single-layered epidermis permits lentiviral infection of ectodermal progenitors, with the perturbation stably maintained during development. To target each cell with a single sgRNA-containing virus particle, we chose infection rates between 2% and 10% (Fig. 1e,f), which are below the expected multiple infection range and minimize the likelihood of double-infected cells20,21. We collected the mouse epidermis at postnatal day 4 (P4) or day 60 (P60) and isolated EGFP-positive, sgRNA-containing cells using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) (Extended Data Fig. 1k). These cells were then processed to generate scRNA-seq libraries alongside sgRNA capture (Fig. 1d).

We generated scRNA-seq libraries of a total of 700,726 cells across the P4 and P60 timepoints. Following stringent filtering for cells with low unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts and for cells without sgRNA capture, we obtained 196,704 P4 epidermal cells and 197,581 P60 cells expressing a single sgRNA. This accounts for a robust coverage of 273 (P4) and 274 (P60) cells on average per sgRNA (Fig. 2a–g and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). As previously shown15, the in vivo single-cell CRISPR screening approach enables us to detect the major epidermal cell populations, including Krt14-positive epidermal stem cells, Krt10-positive suprabasal cells, upper hair follicles, inner and outer bulge stem cells, sebaceous glands and immune cells such as T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells (Fig. 2b–g).

Maximum and minimum percentages of epidermal stem cells are depicted by dashed lines. The black box highlights microproteins with distinct differences in epidermal stem cell proportions. UHF, upper hair follicle; EpSCs, epidermal stem cells; MP, macrophages; DC, dendritic cells.

The epidermis provides a powerful model for studying tissue dynamics and the intricate balance between proliferation and differentiation21,26,27. First, we assessed the overall effect of microproteins on epidermal proliferation using the conventional CRISPR screening readout, considering sgRNAs representation at P4 compared with the initial library (T0). While microprotein perturbations directly cause microprotein loss, uORF targeting may act through loss of the encoded microprotein or altered translational regulation of the main ORF. Among the top depleted P4 candidates, we found sgRNAs targeting the uORFs or the 5’ untranslated regions (5’UTR) of several cancer-associated genes, including Mdm2, Hras and Pten (Fig. 2h). These cancer genes are known to harbour complex 5’UTRs. For example, the oncogene Mdm2 is reported to toggle between two transcript isoforms, where one contains two uORFs, resulting in a poorly translated mRNA28. Furthermore, the tumour suppressor Pten contains several N-terminal extensions and uORFs that also control the ratio of these proteoforms29,30,31 (Extended Data Fig. 1f). By contrast, perturbation of the microproteins Gm10177, Gm5844 and Gm14398 led to a strong enrichment, suggesting that these microproteins negatively impact epidermal development. In addition, perturbation of Gm7239, a recently identified nuclear microprotein in the liver32, was similarly among the top enriched microproteins (Fig. 2h).

summary: Using an in vivo single-cell CRISPR screen, Valdivia-Francia et al. identify the pseudogene Gm10076, which encodes a microprotein identical to the ribosomal protein RPL41 and regulates ribosome biogenesis.
